specPoints.text: Core practical 3: investigate how insulating materials can be charged by friction (physics only)

primer.text: This core practical hangs a rubbed polythene rod from a cradle and brings other rubbed rods close — never touching — to watch attraction and repulsion do the talking. Rod material is the variable under test; rubbing time, cloth and rod length are controlled. The analysis sorts polythene and acetate onto opposite charge signs.

lessons.title: Apparatus, variables & method
lessons.opening: The set-up is deliberately delicate: a polythene rod hangs from a cradle on nylon string so the smallest electrostatic nudge can swing it. Each test rod is rubbed with its own cloth and brought close without contact — any touch would drain the charge and end the experiment.
keyPoints: The experiment tests how friction charges rods of different insulating materials.
The rod material is the independent variable; the charge gained is the dependent one.
Rubbing time, cloth type and rod length are the controlled variables.
A polythene rod hangs from a cradle on nylon string so it can swing freely.
Test rods are brought near, never touched, or the charge would leak away.

low.restatement: Rub a rod with a cloth, hang another rod on a string, and watch whether they push apart or pull together.
low.analogy: Two magnets on strings: hold one still, bring the other near, and the swing tells you the sign.
low.examPointer: Name the variables precisely — independent (rod material), dependent (charge), controls (time, cloth, length).

medium.restatement: The cradle isolates the hanging rod from hand contact, and the no-touch rule protects the transferred charge from leaking to earth through fingers.
medium.analogy: A held-back detective at a crime scene: observing from a distance keeps the evidence intact.
medium.examPointer: Apparatus questions expect the full suspension kit: cradle, nylon string, wooden stand.

options.explanation: Rubbing time is controlled, not varied.
The cloth is kept the same on purpose.
Different rod materials are what the experiment varies.
Deflection is an observation, not the set variable.
The charge produced by rubbing is what the experiment measures.
Temperature is neither varied nor measured here.
Rod length is controlled.
String tension is not the measured quantity.

check.stem: Why must the rods never touch during the test?

options.explanation: Nothing in the procedure heats the rods.
The string never comes under such a load.
Contact does not create charge.

options.text: contact would discharge them and the forces would vanish
options.explanation: Touching lets the charge flow away, removing the observed forces.

check.stem: The polythene rod is suspended so that it can:

options.explanation: Heating plays no role.

options.text: swing freely when a force acts
options.explanation: The cradle and nylon string let the rod respond to tiny electrostatic forces.
Contact with the cradle would discharge it.
The rod hangs clear of the stand.

check.stem: Which control keeps the charge transferred comparable between trials?

options.text: rubbing for the same time with the same cloth
options.explanation: Both time and cloth are held fixed so the trials compare fairly.
Length is a control — it must not vary.
The cloth stays the same.
Varying the rubbing undermines the comparison.

check.stem: List the equipment used to suspend the test rod.
check.modelAnswer: A cradle hung by nylon string from a wooden stand.

check.stem: State the aim of this core practical.
check.modelAnswer: The investigation asks how friction can charge insulating materials.

check.stem: Explain why the ends of the rods must not be handled after rubbing.
check.modelAnswer: Fingers would earth the rubbed ends, draining the charge just gathered and leaving no force to observe.

check.stem: A student rubs the acrylic rod for twice as long as the polythene one. Identify the variable ignored and the effect on the comparison.
check.modelAnswer: The controlled rubbing time was ignored; the extra charge on the acrylic would exaggerate its deflection and bias the comparison.

lessons.title: Analysis: polythene vs acetate & evaluating
lessons.opening: The result table writes itself: a rubbed polythene rod gains electrons from its cloth and charges negatively, while an rubbed acetate rod loses them and charges positively. The hanging rod's response sorts every test rod — rotating away means like charge, swinging in means opposite. Careful evaluation then covers draughts, misread swings and a numerical upgrade.
keyPoints: Rubbing transfers electrons from one insulator onto the other.
A rubbed polythene rod gains electrons and charges negatively.
A rubbed acetate rod loses electrons and charges positively.
Repulsion by the hanging rod means like charges; attraction means opposite ones.
Small deflections can be misread; more rubbing transfers more charge and a clearer swing.
A numerical variant counts paper circles picked up, giving graphable data.

low.restatement: Polythene goes negative, acetate goes positive; same-sign rods push apart, opposite-sign rods pull together.
low.analogy: Two people wearing matching football shirts push away from each other's fans; rivals mix freely.
low.examPointer: Answer in electron language: gained electrons = negative, lost electrons = positive.

medium.restatement: The observed swing is a force comparison, so its direction is trustworthy but its size is qualitative — which is why the paper-circle variant adds numbers.
medium.analogy: Reading a compass versus a protractor: direction is reliable, magnitude needs an instrument.
medium.examPointer: Evaluation marks sit in two places: shielding from draughts/vibrations, and the numerical dependent variable.

check.stem: A polythene rod rubbed with a cloth becomes negative because:

options.text: protons transfer onto it from the cloth
options.explanation: Protons never leave nuclei.

options.text: electrons transfer onto it from the cloth
options.explanation: The polythene gains the cloth's electrons and so turns negative.

options.text: it loses electrons to the cloth
options.explanation: That would leave it positive — the acetate behaviour.
Only electrons move; positive charge never travels.

check.stem: An acetate rod rubbed with a cloth becomes positive because it:

options.explanation: Gaining electrons is the negative case.
Protons stay fixed.
Losing negative charge leaves the acetate positive.
If it kept them all it would stay neutral.

check.stem: The hanging polythene rod rotates away from a test rod. The test rod is:

options.explanation: An uncharged rod would not repel.
Opposite signs attract.
An earthed rod would not push the hanging one away.
Like charges repel, so the test rod is also negative.

check.stem: Attraction to the hanging polythene rod shows the test rod's charge is:

options.explanation: Opposite charges attract.
Like charges repel.
An uncharged rod produces no such direct electrostatic repulsion-or-attraction pair in this test.
Charge is not created by proximity.

check.stem: The numerical improvement swaps the dependent variable for:

options.explanation: Temperature is irrelevant here.

options.text: the number of paper circles picked up
options.explanation: Counting circles turns the observation into data.
Angle alone is not the recorded upgrade described.
Mass loss is not measurable at this scale.

check.stem: State what happens to electrons when two insulators are rubbed together.
check.modelAnswer: Electrons transfer from one insulator onto the other, leaving one negative and the other positive.

check.stem: Give two evaluation points for this experiment.
check.modelAnswer: Shield the set-up from draughts and vibrations, and rub longer when deflections are too small to read confidently.

check.stem: Explain why an object that loses electrons becomes positively charged.
check.modelAnswer: A neutral object scores zero; removing an electron subtracts a negative charge, and 0 − (−1) = +1, so the remainder is positive.

check.stem: In the paper-circle variant, rod X lifts eight circles and rod Y lifts three. Which rod charged more, and what improvement made the comparison possible?
check.modelAnswer: Rod X charged more; turning a directional observation into counted circles gave numerical data that supports graphing and firmer conclusions.

glossary.definition: The quantity the experimenter changes — here, the rod material.
The quantity measured — here, the charge gained by the rod.
The suspension loop that lets the hanging rod swing freely.
The loss of stored charge through contact with another object.
